newsitem.title: FRANCE: ABSat sees 1999 breakeven, more investment.
newsitem.headline: ABSat sees 1999 breakeven, more investment.

text.p: ABSat, AB Productions' digital satellite television service, should break even during 1999, its chairman Claude Berda said in an interview published on Thursday.
He told the daily newspaper Le Figaro that his company had planned investment of 600 million francs, particularly to continue buying programmes and production companies.
"ABSat should reach breakeven during 1999. We have plans to invest 600 million francs in this project and our cash reserves are still well above this amount," Berda said.
He reiterated that he aims to have 75,000 ABSat subscribers by the end of this year.
By then, there would be 600,000 digital television subscribers in France, he said.

"Up to now we have sold 10,000 decoders, of which 7,000 were sold in March, and we have ordered 20,000 more for April and May. As of today, we have more than 4,600 subscriptions, of which over two-thirds came in just in March," he said.

ABSat, whose parent company distributes some of France's most successful television series, is the third digital satellite television service in France, rivalling Canal Plus's CanalSatellite and Television Par Satellite (TPS), controlled by private terrestrial television station M6 and its parents.
Berda said the French market could support three offerings.

"When we decided 18 months ago to go into digital, we did so following a simple observation -- contrary to Germany, France has an extremely limited television offering. Most French homes only receive the five uncoded terrestrial channels. However, the success of Canal Plus showed that the public was prepared to pay for an extra programme offering," he said.
Asked if ABSat would envisage an accord on decoders with TPS similar to the one it recently concluded with CanalSatellite, Berda said ABSat used the same satellite and the same access control as TPS.

"Following the accord with Canal Plus, our decoder is the only one technically able to receive the three offerings. A simple commercial accord with TPS would, out of concern for the television viewer's comfort, allow the three services to be received on a single decoder."

TPS and Canalsatellite have been locked in battle over whose decoder should be used by all French digital television subscribers. Canalsatellite and ABSat recently agreed to use a common software, simulcrypt, for their decoders.
